Since joining Corgi last month, my entire perception of work and success has changed. The "997" culture is real. And it works. I'm not the only one doing it. Everyone on the team is in the office the same hours, grinding the same 7 days a week. At first I thought it would burn me out. Instead, it's the opposite. I've never felt more locked in, more aligned, more part of something bigger than myself. This is how Corgi got to where it is. Not from ping-pong tables and "flexible hours," but from a team that decided to go all-in, together, on something worth building. The part that surprised me most? Nobody's complaining. People want to be here. When everyone's rowing in the same direction at the same intensity, the hours stop feeling like a sacrifice and instead they start feeling like momentum. If you want comfort, don't come to Corgi. If you want to build something exponential, this is what it takes.

I moved to the Bay Area with one goal: do more hackathons. So I checked Luma about as often as I checked Instagram. Then Cerebral Valley. Then whatever else I could find. And I still kept hearing about hackathons the same way every time, from someone at another event, mentioning one that had already happened, that had never appeared anywhere I looked. The frustrating part is that Luma is ideally supposed to solve this. Follow enough calendars, attend enough events, and discovery is meant to come to you. I'd signed up for around 15 tech events in a span of 20 days. My feed was still missing hackathons I would have definitely gone to. So I built my own calendar just for fun. Some GitHub Actions, some scraping, and a classifier that decides what actually counts as a hackathon, it reads 9+ independent sources twice a day, including the curated boards themselves, and publishes one calendar you subscribe to once and then forget about. It currently lists 23 upcoming Bay Area hackathons. The best-known Luma hackathon calendar lists 9 (one of which is a pitch competition). Subscribe here: luma.com/hacklist-sf , the site and the calendar feed are both linked from there. And if you find a Bay Area hackathon it missed, genuinely tell me. That's the most useful thing you could send me right now. I only did this for SF and the bay right now because that's where I am. But nothing about it is SF-specific, if this turns out to be useful to even one of you, tell me which hackathon-dense city you want next and I'll get one out.

"How much should we spend on ads?" is the same question every founder I speak to at the Incubator asks me. Wrong question. Best dividend I've seen this year is $0. A five-minute Reddit post. Someone to run a LinkedIn launch. Hand-built cold outbound list. Paid isn't too bad. But paid is a crowded auction where you are competing with everyone on the same creative, bidding against companies with 100x your runway. Organic is a room with no furniture, except the attention to detail. We filled out a 500 person expo at the Incubator with no ad budget. What we had was a CRM I created from scratch and the discipline to actually work it. All the sponsors we had were on a list that somebody actually sat down and created. If you’re pre-PMF, your unfair advantage is not money. It’s that you’re small enough to do things that don’t scale, and that no one big is willing to. What is the cheapest channel that has ever worked for you?

GutGutGoose (YC S26) makes personalized probiotics that engineer the human microbiome. Personalization is the future of healthcare, yet the entire probiotics industry is still operating under a one-size-fits-all premise. The formulations are made without knowing anything about the individual consuming them. Everyone gets the same bacterial strains, the same dosage, and when nothing works, the customer is left to make another guess. They’ve eliminated the guessing by customizing the pill to every single person. Customers send in a stool sample, giving our testing facilities over 5GB of extensive microbiome data. An algorithm uses that data to create a digitized clone of the microbiome, test thousands of bacterial strains against it, and find ones that will colonize and be of benefit. These strains are then compiled into a supply of probiotics. Every 3 months, they test again to see how the microbiome has changed, and use the results to improve the next formula. The longitudinal gut data collected will be used in the future to be able to identify chronic diseases such as Alzheimer’s and dementia, years before they begin to affect the individual.
